newsitem.title: USA: Merck, Bristol-Myers stock off on cholesterol drug war.
newsitem.headline: Merck, Bristol-Myers stock off on cholesterol drug war.

text.p: The stock of Warner-Lambert Co. surged and those of its rivals Merck and Co. Inc., and Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. tumbled Wednesday as competition heated up in the billion dollar market for drugs that reduce cholesterol.
The market action followed the release of data suggesting Warner-Lambert's entry in the cholesterol fighting arena was winning a better-than-expected reception.
The data got the attention of Wall Street Wednesday when some analysts changed their opinions of companies in the market.

Warner-Lambert, citing data from pharmaceutical market research firm IMS, said its drug, called Lipitor, had 10.7 percent of new prescriptions in the United States for all cholesterol-lowering drugs in the week ended March 28. That was up from 9.5 percent the previous week.
"We feel the uptake on Lipitor is going to be stronger than anticipated," Merrill Lynch analyst Stephen Buermann said.

Merrill also cited its own research, a survey of physicians that showed stronger-than-expected early enthusiasm for Lipitor. Merrill said it expects Lipitor to gain the largest share of the market's growth.
The report projected that Merck's share of the revenue from the market for cholesterol-reducing drugs would fall to about 41 percent in 2001 from about 72 percent in 1996.
Lipitor was launched in the United States in late February and heralded as the most potent of the class of cholesterol-lowering drugs known as statins.
Clinical studies have show that the statin drugs can prevent heart attacks and lower the risk of death from heart attacks.
Merck's top-selling drug is the statin Zocor, which had $2.8 billion in worldwide sales in 1996. An earlier generation Merck statin, Mevacor, had sales of $1.3 billion in 1996.
Bristol-Myers makes the statin drug Pravachol, which had $1.1 billion in 1996 sales.
Swiss drug maker Novartis AG also makes a statin drug, Lescol.
Merrill Lynch downgraded its near- and long-term ratings on Merck to accumulate from buy. It upgraded its near- and long-term ratings on Warner-Lambert to buy from accumulate.
Analysts at Alex. Brown and Morgan Stanley also downgraded Merck and recommended investors buy Warner-Lambert shares.

Merck, one of the 30 stocks in the Dow Jones industrial average, fell $3.75 to close at $81.50 and topped the New York Stock Exchange's list of most active shares with volume of more than 8.3 million shares traded.

Bristol-Myers fell $2.625 to $59.375, while Warner-Lambert gained $2 to $94.75, also on the NYSE. Pfizer Inc., Warner-Lambert's marketing partner for Lipitor, gave up earlier gains and was down $2 to close at $84.
Rodman & Renshaw analyst Mario Corso and other analysts said they thought the market was large enough and growing rapidly enough to absorb the competition.
"After the dust settles, the Lipitor launch will have very little effect ... on the financial performance for Merck," said Aros Securities analyst David Maris.
He cited Merck's broad drug offerings and upcoming products including its Propecia treatment for hair loss and drugs for fighting asthma and migraine headaches.

The new drugs are considered important to Merck's need to offset the expiration starting in the year 2000 of its patents for the heart drug Vasotec and anti-ulcer drug Pepcid. Mevacor and the heart drug Prinivil go off patent in the U.S. in 2001.
Analysts said they also expected sales forces at Merck and Bristol-Myers to start aggressively marketing their drugs in light of the Lipitor launch.
"I think you're going to see both companies undertake some effort to counteract the Lipitor start," Corso said.
